title: Basic Concepts of Economics
tagline: Factors of production and their rewards, production and consumption, and the vocabulary of the subject.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: Every subject has a working vocabulary, and economics is no exception. Before the course can study economies, it must fix the words that describe how output is made and shared: the factors of production and the rewards that draw them out, the difference between production and consumption, and the ideas of utility and demand that organise economic discussion. This chapter treats those concepts as tools rather than trivia. Each one exists to answer a question the syllabus keeps asking — what goes into production, who receives the output, and how decisions about both are expressed — and each will be used in every chapter that follows.

learningOutcomes: List the four factors of production with the reward each earns.
Explain what land, labour, capital and enterprise contribute to production.
Distinguish production from consumption and from distribution.
Define utility and show how production creates it.
Use the basic vocabulary of economics accurately in answers.
Use the syllabus’s basic economic terms — including sustainable consumption, value, price, income and wealth — precisely and in context.

blocks.text: Everything produced draws on four inputs, and economics names them factors of production. Land is all that nature provides without human making — fields, minerals, water, forests. Labour is human effort, physical and mental, applied to production. Capital is whatever human beings have made to help produce more: tools, machines, buildings, and the finance that buys them. Enterprise is the human ability that combines the other three — the judgement to bring land, labour and capital together in one venture and to bear the risk of doing so. Each factor is rewarded for its contribution: rent to land, wages to labour, interest to capital and profit to enterprise. The rewards are not charity but the price that keeps each factor available for production.

blocks.caption: The factors of production, their contributions and rewards
rows: Natural resources: fields, minerals, water, forests
Organisation of the other three, and risk-bearing

blocks.text: Land, in economics, is nature’s contribution in its original state: the farmer’s field, the miner’s ore, the river’s water and the forest’s timber all count, and so does the site on which a shop stands. Its rewards are rent, paid to whoever owns it, and its supply is fixed by nature — human beings can conserve land, irrigate it or exhaust it, but they cannot make more of it. Labour is the human factor: the weaver at the loom, the teacher in the classroom, the engineer at the drawing board. Its reward is wages, and unlike land, its supply depends on population, skill and the choices people make about work and leisure. The productivity of both factors decides an economy’s output: fertile land feeds, and skilled labour multiplies what any land or machine can produce.

items: Land is fixed in supply, its quality varies, and its rewards depend on location and fertility alike.
Land can be improved by irrigation and husbandry or destroyed by erosion and pollution — stewardship matters.
Labour is heterogeneous: skill, training and health make one hour of labour differ enormously from another.
Wages reflect productivity, skill scarcity and the strength of the worker’s bargaining position.

learn.title: Capital and enterprise: the produced factors

blocks.text: Capital is distinctive because it is itself produced: a machine is made by other machines and other labour, using output that could have been consumed instead. That sacrifice — forgoing present consumption to build tools for future production — is what earns capital its reward of interest. Capital comes in forms that a student should be able to name: fixed capital such as machinery and buildings that last years, and working capital such as raw materials and cash that turn over within a season. Enterprise is the scarcest factor: the person who decides what to produce, arranges the other three factors, and carries the risk that the venture fails. Profit is enterprise’s reward, and it is paid last — after rent, wages and interest — which is precisely why it is also the reward for bearing the uncertainty that the other factors refuse.

items.meaning: Produced aids that last through many production cycles, such as machinery and buildings.
items.context: Fixed capital is bought once and used for years, its cost spread as it works.

items.meaning: Raw materials, stock and cash consumed within a single cycle of production.
items.context: A baker’s flour and fuel are working capital; the oven is fixed capital.

items.meaning: The factor that organises the others and bears the risk of the venture.
items.context: Enterprise is rewarded with profit, paid after all other factors.

items.meaning: Accepting the possibility that the venture’s revenue will fall short of its costs.
items.context: Risk-bearing is why profit exists at all — it pays for uncertainty, not for effort alone.

blocks.text: Production, in economic terms, is not the making of matter but the creation of utility — the quality that makes a good or service useful and wanted. Cotton becomes cloth because someone spins and weaves it, and the cloth has greater utility than the boll; wheat becomes flour, flour becomes bread, and each stage adds the utility that buyers pay for. Services create utility too: a teacher’s hour has utility for the student, a doctor’s diagnosis for the patient, without any object being made. Consumption is the end of that process — the use of the good or service that satisfies the want and destroys or wears out its utility. Between them lies distribution, the movement of goods to consumers, and the three together are the activities every economy performs.

items: Production creates form utility: raw material becomes a finished, usable good.
Transport creates place utility: goods move to where they are wanted.
Storage creates time utility: harvests reach consumers in the months when nothing is harvested.
Services create utility of their own: teaching, healing and carrying all satisfy wants without making objects.

learn.title: Putting the vocabulary to work: demand and value

blocks.text: With the factors and the activities fixed, one more idea completes the introductory vocabulary: demand. Demand is not mere desire — it is desire backed by the ability and willingness to pay, at a given price and time. A person may desire a car and have no money for it; the desire is real but it is not demand, and it moves no factory. This precision matters because the entire course reasons from demand: firms plan production around it, governments forecast revenue from it, and the trade balance reflects it at national scale. Value, similarly, is not a moral judgement but what a good commands in exchange because it is useful, scarce and costly to produce. Holding these definitions sharply is the difference between economic writing and general commentary.

items.text: Sunlight is useful but not scarce and not produced, so it has no price and enters no market.
items.note: Utility alone does not create demand or value — scarcity and cost must join it.

items.text: A student desires a laptop, can afford it, and plans to buy it this month: this is demand.
items.note: Desire plus ability plus willingness to pay at a given time — all three, or it is not demand.

learn.title: The syllabus’s basic terms, used correctly

blocks.text: Beyond the four factors and the production chain, the syllabus prescribes a working vocabulary that every answer is expected to use precisely. Wants are the desires whose satisfaction makes people act; goods are material objects that satisfy wants, and services are the immaterial activities that do — transport, teaching, repair. Utility is the want-satisfying power of a good or service, value is what something is worth in terms of other goods or money, and price is that value expressed in money in a particular market. Production is the process that creates utility or form, place or time value in goods and services, and consumption is the using up of that utility in satisfying wants. Sustainable consumption is consumption that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs — the term that ties everyday buying to the resource base. The factors of production — land, labour, capital and enterprise — are the inputs whose services production pays for, and income is the reward a factor earns. Saving is income not spent on consumption, wealth is the stock of assets accumulated from past savings, and welfare is the well-being that all this activity is ultimately meant to raise. An economy is the whole system of production, distribution and consumption working inside a territory, and the market is the setting where buyers and sellers meet. Precision matters because examiners distinguish neighbouring terms: value versus price, income versus wealth, goods versus services — each pair answers a different question.

Price is value expressed in money in a market
Income is a flow earned per period
Wealth is a stock accumulated over time
Goods are material things satisfying wants

keyPoints: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit, paid in that order of seniority.
Land is fixed in supply and its reward is rent; labour’s reward is wages and depends on productivity and skill.
Capital is produced aid — fixed and working — and earns interest for the consumption it postpones.
Enterprise organises the other factors, bears the risk, and is rewarded with profit paid last.
Production creates utility — form, place or time — and services create utility without making objects.
Consumption is the final use that ends a good’s economic journey.
Demand is desire backed by ability and willingness to pay at a given price and time.
Value in economics means what a good commands in exchange, not what it is morally worth.
examFocus: Name the four factors with their rewards in one table-like sentence — the pairing is where marks are lost.
Explain why capital earns interest: it is produced by foregoing consumption, so it must be paid for waiting.
Distinguish fixed from working capital with a two-example contrast.
Show enterprise as risk-bearing, not merely as ownership, and connect it to profit being paid last.
Explain utility through the three kinds — form, place and time — with an example each.
Define demand strictly: desire without ability to pay is not demand, and say what it fails to move.

vocabulary.meaning: Any input used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital or enterprise.
vocabulary.context: Each factor earns a distinct reward, and the pairing is examined constantly.

vocabulary.meaning: The reward paid for the use of land and other natural resources.
vocabulary.context: Rent is paid to landowners because land’s supply cannot be increased by human effort.

vocabulary.meaning: The reward paid for physical and mental labour.
vocabulary.context: Wages follow productivity and skill, which is why training raises them.

vocabulary.meaning: The reward paid for the use of capital.
vocabulary.context: Interest repays the postponement of consumption that produced the capital.

vocabulary.meaning: The reward of enterprise, paid after rent, wages and interest for bearing risk.
vocabulary.context: Profit exists because someone must be paid for uncertainty the other factors refuse.

vocabulary.meaning: The quality that makes a good or service useful and wanted.
vocabulary.context: Production is the creation of utility — form, place or time.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a factor of production with its reward?
questions.explanation: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and enterprise earns profit. The other three options rotate the pairs, which is the commonest slip in this topic.
questions.commonMistake: Memorising the factors but shuffling the rewards — learn the four pairs as one list.

questions.prompt: Which of these is capital in the economic sense?
options: A machine made to produce goods
Money in a savings account used for spending
A gift of grain to a neighbour
questions.answer: A machine made to produce goods
questions.explanation: Capital is produced aid used in further production: machinery, buildings, tools and the finance invested in them. Money spent on consumption or held as ornament does not help produce anything, and a gift consumes rather than produces.
questions.commonMistake: Calling all money capital — money becomes capital only when it is invested in productive aid.

options: The creation of utility in goods and services
The manufacture of tangible objects only
The sale of goods in a market
questions.answer: The creation of utility in goods and services
questions.explanation: Economic production is whatever makes goods and services useful and available — spinning cotton into cloth is production, and so is teaching a class. Manufacturing, purchase and sale are particular stages, and purchase alone creates nothing usable.
questions.commonMistake: Restricting production to factories, which excludes the services that form a growing part of output.

questions.prompt: Demand differs from a mere want because demand:
options: Is backed by ability and willingness to pay at a given price
Is always stronger than a want
Refers to the want of a whole nation
questions.answer: Is backed by ability and willingness to pay at a given price
questions.explanation: Demand is effective desire: wanting, being able to pay, and being willing to pay now. Without the ability to pay, a want moves no production and therefore does not qualify as demand.
questions.commonMistake: Equating demand with desire, which would predict production of everything anyone has ever wanted.

questions.prompt: Complete: the four factors of production are land, labour, ________ and ________ , and they are rewarded respectively by rent, wages, interest and profit.
questions.explanation: The four factors and their four rewards form one list, and the order of the rewards — rent, wages, interest, profit — also mirrors their seniority of claim on output.
questions.commonMistake: Substituting organisation or money for enterprise or capital; the syllabus terms are fixed.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between fixed capital and working capital, with an example of each.
questions.answer: Fixed capital consists of produced aids that last through many cycles of production, such as machinery, tools and buildings; it is bought once and used for years. Working capital is the stock of raw materials, fuel and cash consumed within a single cycle, such as a baker’s flour and sugar. Fixed capital wears out slowly and its cost is spread over its life; working capital is replaced again and again as production runs.
questions.explanation: The distinction turns on duration of use, and the answer should carry one clean example of each plus the consequence — slow replacement versus constant replacement — which is what proves the difference is understood.
questions.commonMistake: Defining working capital as money alone; it is the whole cycle of materials and cash, not just the cash.

questions.prompt: What is utility? Name the three ways production creates it.
questions.answer: Utility is the quality that makes a good or service useful and wanted, and production is the creation of it. Production creates form utility by turning raw material into a finished good — cotton into cloth. Transport creates place utility by moving goods to where they are wanted, and storage creates time utility by holding harvests for months when nothing is harvested. Services such as teaching and healing create utility of their own without making any object at all.
questions.explanation: The definition must connect utility to want satisfaction, and the three kinds must arrive with an example each — form, place and time — because the syllabus expects the classification, not just the word.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing utility with use: a good can have utility while lying unsold, but it has no value in exchange until someone demands it.

questions.prompt: Explain why profit is paid to enterprise after rent, wages and interest, and what it rewards.
questions.answer: Profit is the reward of enterprise, and it is paid last because the other factors contract for certainty first: the landowner receives rent whether the venture thrives or fails, the worker receives wages for the hours worked, and the lender receives interest on the capital lent. Enterprise keeps what remains only after all three have been settled, and receives nothing at all if the venture fails. That order is not injustice but the price of risk-bearing: profit is the payment for the person who organises land, labour and capital together, decides what to produce and how, and carries the uncertainty that the other three factors refuse to carry. In good years profit is large precisely because in bad years it is negative — the entrepreneur repays earlier losses out of later gains, and the possibility of that repayment is what draws people into organising production at all. Without it, new ventures would not be attempted and the economy’s output would stay within the safe boundaries its existing factors preferred.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the order of payment explained as a consequence of contractual certainty, and profit defined as payment for risk-bearing and organisation. The final link — that negative profit in bad years is the mirror of positive profit in good — shows why the reward must exist.
questions.commonMistake: Calling profit the reward for hard work alone, which would not explain why wage-earners who work equally hard do not receive it.

questions.prompt: “Land is fixed in supply, yet its reward keeps changing.” Explain with reference to what determines rent.
questions.answer: The quantity of land cannot be increased by human effort — no economy can manufacture another river valley — but its reward is not fixed, because rent depends not on supply alone but on what land can produce and where it lies. Fertile land near a growing city earns rising rent because the crops and the sites on it serve more buyers each year; the same plot a generation earlier, remote and unirrigated, earned almost nothing. Irrigation, roads and market access raise the earning power of a fixed plot, so its rent rises with demand while its supply stays constant; erosion, pollution and depletion do the reverse. The lesson generalises: for any factor whose supply cannot respond quickly, price is driven almost entirely by demand, which is why urban land rents climb while wages for common skills adjust slowly too. Land’s fixed supply also explains its stewardship problem: rent rewards use, so owners have incentive to extract, and society needs rules to keep the fixed resource from being exhausted.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate physical quantity from economic scarcity: supply is fixed, but rent is set by demand for what the land can yield, moved by fertility, location and access. Examples of urban and irrigated land make the mechanism concrete, and the generalisation to factors with inelastic supply shows analytical reach.
questions.commonMistake: Concluding that rent must be constant because land is fixed — that confuses quantity with earning power.

questions.prompt: A farmer uses a bullock cart; later a tractor; later a fleet of trucks with a warehouse. Trace how the factors of production and their rewards change across the three stages.
questions.answer: In the first stage the factors are simple: the farmer’s own land, personal labour, and a bullock cart that is fixed capital produced earlier by a carpenter. The rewards are rent to the landlord if the land is taken on lease, wages if hired help drives the cart, interest on whatever borrowing bought the bullocks, and whatever remains is the farmer’s profit as enterprise. In the second stage the tractor replaces animal power: capital deepens, the interest bill rises, and labour demand falls because one driver now does the work of several — the technique has shifted towards the capital-intensive side of the how-to-produce question. In the third stage the farmer becomes an enterprise: trucks and a warehouse multiply fixed capital, hired managers and drivers add wage labour on a larger scale, storage creates time utility that earns better prices, and profit now carries real risk — a breakdown or a price fall can wipe out the year. Across the stages the land changes little; what changes is the capital–labour ratio, the size of the interest obligation, and the share of reward that flows to enterprise rather than to wages. The same four factors are present throughout — only their proportions, and therefore the distribution of rewards among them, have been transformed.
questions.explanation: The tracing must keep the four factors visible in every stage and show what actually changes: the capital–labour ratio, the interest burden, and the shift of reward towards enterprise. Connecting the middle stage to the how-to-produce question ties the answer back to the course’s central problem.
questions.commonMistake: Describing modernisation as simply “more machines”, without tracking which factors grew, which shrank, and how the rewards moved.

questions.prompt: What is sustainable consumption? State why the term appears among the basic economic terms.
questions.answer: Sustainable consumption is the use of goods and services at a rate that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own — it means consuming within the renewal limits of the resources that supply the goods. The term appears among the basic terms because consumption cannot be defined only as the using up of utility: economics also asks whether the using-up is repeatable. A household that exhausts its groundwater or soil to consume more today reduces tomorrow’s production possibilities, so sustainable consumption links the individual act of consumption to the economy’s long-run resource base — and it is the one basic term that carries a judgement about time rather than only a definition.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the definition in terms of present versus future generations and the reason it belongs: consumption has a time dimension that ties household choice to the economy’s resource base.
questions.commonMistake: Defining it as “recycling” or “buying less” — sustainability is about intergenerational capacity, not about a particular habit.
